subjective.question: Define managerial accounting and state its main objectives.
subjective.answer: Managerial accounting is the process of identifying, measuring, analyzing, interpreting and communicating financial and non-financial information to managers so that they can plan, control and make decisions for the organization. Its main objectives are: (1) to provide relevant information for decision making, (2) to assist in planning and formulating budgets, (3) to help in controlling operations by comparing actual results with plans, (4) to measure the performance of departments and managers, and (5) to assist in determining product costs and setting prices.

subjective.question: Differentiate between financial accounting and managerial accounting. (Any five points)
subjective.answer: (1) Users: financial accounting reports to external users (shareholders, banks, government), while managerial accounting reports to internal users (managers). (2) Rules: financial accounting must follow GAAP, while managerial accounting follows no prescribed rules. (3) Time focus: financial accounting is historical, while managerial accounting is future-oriented. (4) Compulsion: financial accounting is legally required, while managerial accounting is optional. (5) Detail: financial accounting reports on the whole organization, while managerial accounting focuses on segments, products and departments. (6) Reporting period: financial statements are prepared periodically (yearly/quarterly), while managerial reports are prepared whenever managers need them.

subjective.question: Define prime cost and conversion cost, and compute both for the following data: direct materials Rs. 40,000, direct labor Rs. 25,000, manufacturing overhead Rs. 15,000.
subjective.answer: Prime cost is the sum of all direct costs of production, i.e. direct materials plus direct labor. Conversion cost is the cost incurred to convert raw materials into finished goods, i.e. direct labor plus manufacturing overhead. Prime cost = 40,000 + 25,000 = Rs. 65,000. Conversion cost = 25,000 + 15,000 = Rs. 40,000.

subjective.question: Distinguish between product costs and period costs, giving two examples of each.
subjective.answer: Product costs are the costs incurred to manufacture a product — direct materials, direct labor and manufacturing overhead. They are stored in inventory and expensed as cost of goods sold only when the product is sold. Period costs are not part of manufacturing; they are expensed in full in the period in which they are incurred. Examples of product costs: raw materials consumed, factory wages. Examples of period costs: sales commission, office salaries, advertising.

subjective.question: Define sunk cost, opportunity cost and relevant cost with one example each.
subjective.answer: Sunk cost: a cost that has already been incurred in the past and cannot be changed by any future decision, e.g. the purchase price of a machine already bought; it is irrelevant for decision making. Opportunity cost: the benefit forgone when one alternative is chosen over another, e.g. the rent forgone by using one's own building for the factory. Relevant cost: a future cost that differs among alternatives and therefore affects a decision, e.g. the additional material cost of accepting a special order.

subjective.question: Explain fixed cost, variable cost and mixed cost, describing the behavior of each in total and per unit.
subjective.answer: Fixed cost remains constant in total within the relevant range regardless of the activity level (e.g. factory rent), but fixed cost per unit decreases as production increases. Variable cost changes in total in direct proportion to the activity level (e.g. direct materials), while variable cost per unit remains constant. Mixed (semi-variable) cost contains both a fixed and a variable element (e.g. a telephone bill with a fixed monthly charge plus per-call charges); it increases with activity but not in direct proportion.

subjective.question: Using the high-low method, separate the following mixed cost into its fixed and variable components and estimate the total cost at 8,000 units: at 10,000 units the total cost is Rs. 85,000 and at 6,000 units the total cost is Rs. 61,000.
Define contribution margin and contribution margin ratio, and derive the formula for the break-even point in units.
subjective.answer: Contribution margin is the excess of sales revenue over total variable costs; it is the amount available to cover fixed costs and then provide profit. Contribution margin ratio = contribution margin ÷ sales. At the break-even point, total contribution margin is exactly equal to total fixed costs and profit is zero. Therefore: Break-even units × contribution margin per unit = total fixed costs, so Break-even point (units) = Total fixed costs ÷ Contribution margin per unit.

subjective.question: A company sells its product for Rs. 50 per unit. Variable cost is Rs. 30 per unit and total fixed costs are Rs. 100,000. Compute: (a) the break-even point in units and in sales rupees, and (b) the units required to earn a profit of Rs. 60,000.
subjective.answer: Contribution margin per unit = 50 − 30 = Rs. 20. (a) Break-even units = 100,000 ÷ 20 = 5,000 units. Break-even sales = 5,000 × 50 = Rs. 250,000 (or 100,000 ÷ 40% CM ratio = Rs. 250,000). (b) Required units = (Fixed costs + Target profit) ÷ CM per unit = (100,000 + 60,000) ÷ 20 = 8,000 units.

subjective.question: Define margin of safety and degree of operating leverage, and state the formula of each.
subjective.answer: Margin of safety is the excess of actual (or budgeted) sales over break-even sales; it shows by how much sales can drop before the company starts making a loss. Margin of safety = Actual sales − Break-even sales; Margin of safety ratio = Margin of safety ÷ Actual sales. Degree of operating leverage measures the sensitivity of operating income to a change in sales: Degree of operating leverage = Contribution margin ÷ Operating income. A higher degree means profits rise (and fall) faster with changes in sales volume.

subjective.question: State any five assumptions of cost-volume-profit (CVP) analysis.
subjective.answer: (1) All costs can be separated into fixed and variable components. (2) Selling price per unit remains constant at all volume levels. (3) Variable cost per unit remains constant. (4) Total fixed costs remain constant within the relevant range. (5) Production is equal to sales, i.e. there is no change in inventory levels. (6) In multi-product firms, the sales mix remains constant.

subjective.question: FitDat.com is a newly incorporated company that manufactures a small battery-operated fitness monitor. This hand-held gadget sends data to its user's smartphone during exercise. Virtually all of its sales are expected to be web-based. Its management accountant is studying the two famous costing methods — absorption costing and variable costing — that the company can use to determine its product cost. Under absorption costing, all manufacturing costs, including fixed manufacturing overhead, are treated as product cost and stored in inventory until the inventory is sold. Under variable costing, fixed manufacturing overhead is not included in the cost of inventory; here, fixed manufacturing overhead is treated as a period cost and is expensed during the period in which it is incurred. The company intends to employ the costing method which ensures true and fair reporting of its income in the financial statements. (a) Which costing method, with an increased inventory level, would produce higher income? (2 Marks) (b) Why, in (a) above, would the income be increased? (3 Marks) (c) Which costing method is consistent with cost-volume-profit analysis? (2 Marks) (d) What is the reason behind the consistency discussed in (c) above?
subjective.answer: (a) Absorption costing. (b) Under absorption costing, fixed manufacturing overhead is treated as a product cost and is stored in inventory. When the inventory level increases, a portion of the current period's fixed manufacturing overhead is deferred in closing inventory and carried forward to the next period instead of being charged against the current period's income. As a result, the cost of goods sold is lower and the reported income of the current period is higher. Under variable costing, the entire fixed manufacturing overhead is expensed in the period incurred, whatever the inventory level. (c) Variable costing. (d) CVP analysis is built on the classification of costs by behavior into fixed and variable, and on the contribution margin; under CVP, profit changes only when the sales volume changes. Variable costing uses exactly the same behavior-based classification and treats fixed manufacturing overhead as a period cost, so profit under variable costing also moves only with sales and not with the level of production. Under absorption costing, profit can rise or fall merely because production (and inventory) changes, even when sales are constant, which conflicts with CVP analysis.

subjective.question: Distinguish between absorption costing and variable costing. (Any five points)
subjective.answer: (1) Treatment of fixed manufacturing overhead: absorption costing includes it in product cost; variable costing treats it as a period cost. (2) Inventory valuation: higher under absorption costing; lower under variable costing. (3) Profit behavior: absorption costing profit depends on both production and sales; variable costing profit depends only on sales. (4) When production exceeds sales, absorption costing shows higher profit; when sales exceed production, variable costing shows higher profit. (5) Use: absorption costing is required for external reporting; variable costing is preferred for internal decisions and CVP analysis.

subjective.question: Fixed manufacturing overhead is Rs. 60,000. Production during the period is 12,000 units and sales are 10,000 units. Compute the difference between the income reported under absorption costing and variable costing, and explain it.
subjective.answer: Fixed manufacturing overhead per unit = 60,000 ÷ 12,000 = Rs. 5 per unit. Units added to inventory = 12,000 − 10,000 = 2,000 units. Under absorption costing, fixed overhead deferred in closing inventory = 2,000 × 5 = Rs. 10,000. Therefore absorption costing income is Rs. 10,000 higher than variable costing income, because Rs. 10,000 of the period's fixed overhead is carried in inventory instead of being expensed.

subjective.question: What is a master budget? List its main components in sequence.
subjective.answer: The master budget is the comprehensive financial plan of an organization for a budget period, summarizing all the individual budgets of its segments. Its main components in sequence are: (1) sales budget, (2) production budget, (3) direct materials purchases budget, (4) direct labor budget, (5) manufacturing overhead budget, (6) ending inventory and cost of goods sold budget, (7) selling and administrative expense budget, (8) cash budget, and (9) the budgeted income statement and budgeted balance sheet.

subjective.question: Differentiate between a static budget and a flexible budget, and state two advantages of a flexible budget.
subjective.answer: A static budget is prepared for only one planned level of activity and is not adjusted when the actual activity differs. A flexible budget is designed to change with the level of activity; it shows what costs should have been at the actual level of activity. Advantages of a flexible budget: (1) it provides a fair basis for performance evaluation because actual costs are compared with the budget for the same activity level, and (2) it can be used at any activity level within the relevant range, making planning and control more realistic.

subjective.question: Define standard cost and standard costing, and state its main objectives.
subjective.answer: A standard cost is a carefully predetermined cost that should be incurred under efficient operating conditions for producing one unit (or performing an operation). Standard costing is the technique of setting standards, comparing actual costs with standards, and analyzing the variances. Its main objectives are: (1) to control costs, (2) to evaluate the performance of departments and managers, (3) to simplify inventory valuation and bookkeeping, and (4) to assist in setting budgets and prices.

subjective.question: Define material price variance and material usage variance. Then compute both for the following data: standard price Rs. 5.00 per kg; actual price Rs. 5.20 per kg; actual quantity used 10,500 kg; standard quantity allowed 10,000 kg.
subjective.answer: Material price variance = (Actual price− Standard price) × Actual quantity; it measures the effect of paying more or less than the standard price. Material usage (quantity) variance = (Actual quantity− Standard quantity) × Standard price; it measures the effect of using more or less material than the standard allowed. Price variance = (5.20− 5.00) × 10,500 = 0.20 × 10,500 = Rs. 2,100 unfavorable. Usage variance = (10,500 − 10,000) × 5.00 = 500 × 5 = Rs. 2,500 unfavorable.

subjective.question: Define net present value (NPV) and state its decision rule. Compute the NPV of a project that requires an initial investment of Rs. 500,000 and generates cash inflows of Rs. 150,000 per year for 5 years, given that the cost of capital is 10% and the present value annuity factor for 5 years at 10% is 3.7908.
subjective.answer: Net present value is the difference between the present value of a project's cash inflows (discounted at the cost of capital) and its initial investment. Decision rule: accept the project if NPV is positive, reject it if NPV is negative, because a positive NPV means the project earns more than the required rate of return. Present value of inflows = 150,000 × 3.7908 = Rs. 568,620. NPV = 568,620 − 500,000 = Rs. 68,620. Since the NPV is positive, the project should be accepted.

subjective.question: Define payback period, compute it for an investment of Rs. 500,000 with even annual cash inflows of Rs. 150,000, and state two limitations of this method.
subjective.answer: The payback period is the length of time required for the cumulative cash inflows from a project to recover its initial investment. Payback period = 500,000 ÷ 150,000 = 3.33 years (approximately 3 years and 4 months). Limitations: (1) it ignores the time value of money, and (2) it ignores all cash flows that occur after the payback period, so it does not measure the project's overall profitability.

subjective.question: Define internal rate of return (IRR) and state its decision rule.
subjective.answer: The internal rate of return is the discount rate at which the present value of a project's cash inflows becomes exactly equal to its initial investment, i.e. the rate at which the NPV of the project is zero. Decision rule: accept the project if its IRR is greater than the cost of capital (the hurdle rate), because the project then earns more than the minimum required return; reject it if the IRR is less than the cost of capital.

subjective.question: List any four techniques of capital budgeting and briefly explain each.
subjective.answer: (1) Payback period: the time needed to recover the initial investment from cash inflows; simple but ignores the time value of money. (2) Net present value: discounts all cash flows at the cost of capital and accepts projects with a positive NPV. (3) Internal rate of return: the discount rate that makes NPV zero; accepted if it exceeds the cost of capital. (4) Profitability index: present value of future cash flows divided by the initial investment; accepted if greater than 1. (5) Accounting rate of return: average annual accounting profit divided by the investment, expressed as a percentage.

subjective.question: Define return on investment (ROI). Using the DuPont formula, compute ROI from the following data: operating income Rs. 120,000, sales Rs. 1,000,000, average operating assets Rs. 800,000.
subjective.answer: Return on investment is a measure of the profit earned on the assets invested in a division or project: ROI = Operating income ÷ Average operating assets. By the DuPont formula, ROI = Margin × Turnover. Margin = 120,000 ÷ 1,000,000 = 12%. Turnover = 1,000,000 ÷ 800,000 = 1.25. ROI = 12% × 1.25 = 15%. (Direct check: 120,000 ÷ 800,000 = 15%.)

subjective.question: Define residual income and compute it for the following data: operating income Rs. 120,000, average operating assets Rs. 800,000, minimum required rate of return 12%. Also state one advantage of residual income over ROI.
subjective.answer: Residual income is the operating income earned above the minimum required return on the operating assets: Residual income = Operating income − (Minimum required rate of return × Average operating assets) = 120,000 − (12% × 800,000) = 120,000 − 96,000 = Rs. 24,000. Advantage: unlike ROI, residual income encourages managers to accept every project that earns more than the minimum required rate, because any such project increases residual income; under ROI a manager may reject a profitable project if it lowers the division's overall ROI percentage.

subjective.question: Define management audit and state its main objectives.
subjective.answer: A management audit is a systematic and independent evaluation of the efficiency and effectiveness of the management of an organization — its plans, policies, objectives, organizational structure, systems and controls — carried out to identify weaknesses and suggest improvements. Its main objectives are: (1) to evaluate whether management is achieving the organization's objectives economically and efficiently, (2) to identify deficiencies in policies, procedures and controls, (3) to assess the performance of managers at different levels, (4) to suggest remedial measures and improvements, and (5) to assist top management and the board in better decision making.

subjective.question: State any five areas (scope) covered by a management audit.
subjective.answer: (1) The objectives and plans of the organization and how far they are being achieved. (2) The organizational structure — whether authority and responsibility are clearly defined. (3) Management policies and procedures in areas such as production, marketing, finance and personnel. (4) The system of internal control and internal check. (5) The quality of management information and reporting systems. (6) The utilization of resources — manpower, materials, machines and money — and the performance of different departments.

subjective.question: Differentiate between return on investment (ROI) and residual income. (Any four points)
subjective.answer: (1) Nature: ROI is a ratio expressed as a percentage, while residual income is an absolute amount in rupees. (2) Basis: ROI = operating income ÷ average operating assets; residual income = operating income − (minimum required rate × average operating assets). (3) Decision effect: ROI may lead a manager to reject a project earning above the cost of capital if it reduces the division's ROI; residual income always increases when such a project is accepted. (4) Comparison: ROI is useful for comparing divisions of different sizes, while residual income favors larger divisions because bigger divisions can show larger absolute amounts.

subjective.question: Define the following terms: (a) cost-volume-profit analysis, (b) break-even point, (c) contribution margin, (d) relevant range, (e) flexible budget.
subjective.answer: (a) Cost-volume-profit analysis is the study of the relationships among cost, volume (activity) and profit, used to determine how changes in costs and volume affect a company's operating income. (b) Break-even point is the level of sales (in units or rupees) at which total revenue equals total cost, so the company earns neither profit nor loss. (c) Contribution margin is the excess of sales revenue over total variable costs, available to cover fixed costs and provide profit. (d) Relevant range is the range of activity within which the assumptions about fixed and variable cost behavior remain valid. (e) Flexible budget is a budget that adjusts (flexes) to the actual level of activity, showing the costs that should have been incurred at that activity level.
